docs.title: Export integration logic as a CApp
docs.text: Follow the steps in the Build and Export the Carbon Application guide to build and export the CApp to a specified location.

docs.title: Get the project
docs.text: You can download the ZIP file and extract the contents to get the project code.

docs.title: Run the Integration
docs.text:
To deploy and run the project, refer to the build and run guide or simply use the Run button in the Visual Studio Code extension to run the integration.

You can further refer to the application deployed through the CLI tool. See the instructions on managing integrations from the CLI.

docs.title: Testing the Integration
docs.text:
You can manually publish messages to a RabbitMQ queue via the RabbitMQ management console. Refer to the official RabbitMQ documentation for guidance on accessing the management console. You can use the console to publish messages for testing purposes. However, this approach is not recommended for enterprise-level deployments.

Alternatively, you can use the RabbitMQ (AMQP 1.0) Connector example to insert data programmatically. In this example, we will use the WSO2 MI RabbitMQ (AMQP 1.0) connector to insert data into the RabbitMQ queue.

  1. Save the following payload as data.json:

    {
"queue": "notification-queue",
"message": "Hello World!"
}

  2. Invoke the API using the following curl command:

curl -X POST -d @data.json http://localhost:8290/publishmessage --header "Content-Type:application/json"

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
After inserting a record, you should see a log entry in the WSO2 Integrator: MI console similar to the following:

[2026-02-13 18:32:39,526]  INFO {LogMediator} RabbitMQInboundEP-rabbitmq-inbound-listener-dispatcher-0 - {inboundendpoint:RabbitMQInboundEP} {"text":"Hello World!"}

docs.title: RabbitMQ (AMQP 1.0) Inbound Endpoint Reference
docs.text:
This reference page documents all the configuration parameters supported by the RabbitMQ Inbound Endpoint. These parameters control how the inbound endpoint connects to the RabbitMQ server, what queues it consumes from, the consumer type, message acknowledgment modes, and more. Use this table as a guide when configuring your inbound endpoint to ensure seamless and reliable integration with RabbitMQ. Parameter Name Display Name Description Required Default Value Generic name Event Integration Name A unique name for this RabbitMQ Inbound Endpoint configuration. Yes - sequence Injecting Sequence Name The name of the mediation sequence that will process the consumed RabbitMQ messages. Yes - onError Error Sequence Name The name of the error handling sequence to execute if an error occurs during message consumption or processing. Yes - suspend Suspend Inbound Suspend the inbound endpoint No false Inbound Functional sequential Execute sequentially If enabled, messages will be processed one after the other within the injection sequence, preserving message order. No true coordination Coordination In a clustered environment, set this to true to ensure that only a single worker node is consuming messages from the queue at any given time. No true Basic rabbitmq.server.host.name Server Hosts Specifies the RabbitMQ server hostname(s) or IP address(es) for client connection. For high availability deployments, provide multiple hosts as a comma-separated list (e.g., rabbitmq1.example.com,rabbitmq2.example.com,rabbitmq3.example.com). Single server configuration:

  • Hostname: rabbitmq.example.com - Recommended for production (enables DNS-based failover)
  • IP address: 192.168.1.100 - Direct IP connection (bypasses DNS resolution)
  • localhost: localhost or 127.0.0.1 - For local development and testing only
Multi-server configuration (High Availability):
  • Provide comma-separated list: rabbitmq1.example.com,rabbitmq2.example.com,rabbitmq3.example.com
  • Client automatically attempts connection to each host in sequence until successful
  • Enables automatic failover if the primary broker becomes unavailable
  • All hosts should be part of the same RabbitMQ cluster for proper operation
  • Order matters: hosts are tried in the specified order during connection and reconnection attempts
Best practices:
  • Use hostnames over IPs: Allows infrastructure changes without client reconfiguration
  • List all cluster nodes: Maximizes availability - if one node fails, client can connect to others
  • Geographic considerations: List closest/lowest-latency nodes first for optimal performance
  • Load balancer option: Can use a single load balancer hostname (e.g., rabbitmq-lb.example.com) instead of listing individual nodes, but this creates a single point of failure if the load balancer fails
  • Network segmentation: Ensure all listed hosts are accessible from the client's network segment
Port alignment: If providing multiple hosts, ensure corresponding ports are listed in rabbitmq.server.port in the same order. If only one port is specified, it applies to all hosts. Connection behavior:
  • Client attempts connection to the first host in the list
  • If connection fails, automatically tries the next host
  • Continues through the list until a connection succeeds or all hosts are exhausted
  • After successful connection, if that connection drops, the client retries using the same failover logic
Important: This is a required parameter. For production deployments, always specify multiple hosts for high availability unless using a highly available load balancer. Yes localhost rabbitmq.server.port Server Ports Specifies the RabbitMQ server ports as a comma-separated list (e.g., port1,port2). Default is 5672 for non-SSL. Yes 5672 rabbitmq.queue.name Queue Name The name of the RabbitMQ queue to consume messages from. Yes - rabbitmq.queue.type Type Specifies the type of RabbitMQ queue to interact with. Options:
  • CLASSIC: The traditional RabbitMQ queue type with support for all messaging patterns and features. Offers flexibility and full protocol compatibility but provides limited fault tolerance as queues are stored on a single node. Suitable for development, testing, or non-critical workloads where high availability is not required.
  • QUORUM: A replicated queue type built on the Raft consensus algorithm, providing high availability and data safety through replication across multiple cluster nodes. Automatically handles leader election and failover. Designed for critical workloads requiring message durability and resilience against node failures. Recommended for production environments where message loss is unacceptable. Note: Does not support all classic queue features (e.g., priority queues, message TTL at message level).
  • STREAM: A persistent, append-only log structure optimized for high-throughput, large-volume message flows with non-destructive consumption. Messages are retained on disk and can be consumed multiple times by different consumers from any offset. Ideal for event streaming, audit logs, time-series data, and scenarios requiring message replay or long-term retention. Requires RabbitMQ 3.9+ and uses a different consumption model than traditional queues.
Yes QUORUM rabbitmq.queue.auto.declare Auto Declare If enabled, the inbound endpoint will attempt to declare the queue if it doesn't exist. No true rabbitmq.exchange.name Exchange Name Name of the exchange to bind the queue to. Leave empty to consume directly from the queue. No - rabbitmq.exchange.type Type Defines how the exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules. Options:
  • DIRECT: Routes messages to queues based on an exact match between the routing key and the binding key. Simple and efficient for point-to-point messaging where each message should be delivered to specific queues. Ideal for task distribution and targeted message delivery scenarios.
  • FANOUT: Broadcasts all messages to all bound queues, ignoring routing keys entirely. Every queue bound to the exchange receives a copy of each message. Perfect for publish-subscribe patterns, notifications, and scenarios where the same message needs to reach multiple independent consumers simultaneously.
  • TOPIC: Routes messages based on wildcard pattern matching between the routing key and binding patterns. Binding keys can use wildcards: * (matches exactly one word) and # (matches zero or more words). Enables flexible, hierarchical routing based on multi-part routing keys (e.g., stock.usa.tech). Suitable for complex routing scenarios like log aggregation, multi-criteria filtering, and selective subscription patterns.
  • HEADERS: Routes messages based on matching message header attributes rather than routing keys. Uses the x-match binding argument to specify whether all headers must match or any header match is sufficient. Provides the most flexible routing but with higher overhead. Best for complex routing rules based on multiple message properties or when routing logic cannot be expressed through routing keys alone.
No DIRECT rabbitmq.exchange.auto.declare Auto Declare If enabled, the inbound endpoint will attempt to declare the exchange if it doesn't exist. No true rabbitmq.routing.key Routing Key Routing key for binding the queue to a DIRECT or TOPIC exchange. Queue name is used if omitted. No - User Authentication rabbitmq.connection.sasl.mechanism SASL Mechanism Defines the SASL mechanism to use for connection authentication. Possible values:
  • PLAIN: The default, standard authentication method that transmits username and password credentials in plain text. This mechanism is simple and widely supported but requires secure transport (TLS/SSL) to protect credentials during transmission. When OAuth2 authentication is enabled, the SASL mechanism should be set to PLAIN, as the OAuth2 token is passed as the password field.
  • EXTERNAL: Delegates authentication to an external mechanism, bypassing RabbitMQ's internal user database. This typically works in conjunction with the rabbitmq_auth_backend_external plugin or certificate-based authentication (TLS/SSL mutual authentication). Common use cases:
    • Client Certificate Authentication: The client's identity is extracted from the TLS certificate's Distinguished Name (DN) during the TLS handshake, eliminating the need for username/password credentials.
    • External Authentication Scripts: When using rabbitmq_auth_backend_external, authentication and authorization are delegated to external scripts or programs that can integrate with LDAP, Kerberos, custom databases, or other identity providers.
    This mechanism is suitable for enterprise environments requiring centralized identity management or certificate-based security models.
Security Considerations:
  • PLAIN: Always use with TLS/SSL encryption to prevent credential interception. Never use over unencrypted connections in production environments.
  • EXTERNAL: Requires proper certificate management and PKI infrastructure for certificate-based auth, or secure configuration of external authentication backends. Provides stronger authentication but increases setup and maintenance complexity.
Yes PLAIN rabbitmq.server.user.name Server Username Username for PLAIN authentication. No guest rabbitmq.server.password Server Password Password for PLAIN authentication. No guest rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.enabled OAuth2 Enabled Enable if using OAuth 2.0 (e.g., Client Credentials or Password Grant) for authentication instead of a simple username/password. When OAuth 2.0 is enabled, RabbitMQ validates access tokens presented by clients against a configured authorization server. The OAuth 2.0 plugin uses JWT (JSON Web Token) tokens and can verify them either by validating the token's signature using public keys or by introspecting the token with the authorization server. Please refer to the RabbitMQ OAuth 2.0 plugin documentation for detailed configuration instructions and supported Identity providers. No false rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.token.endpoint Token Endpoint Defines the Identity Provider/Token Service token endpoint URL to generate the access token.

Note

Provide the HTTPS URL for the token endpoint and import the Identity Provider's public certificate into the WSO2 MI client-truststore.jks. See importing SSL certificates to a truststore for instructions on importing the certificate into client-truststore.jks.

No - rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.grant.type Grant Type Defines the OAuth2 grant type to use for token generation. Options:
  • client_credentials: Used for machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication where the application authenticates using its own credentials (client ID and client secret) without user involvement. This is the most common grant type for service-to-service communication and background processes. Recommended for most RabbitMQ integration scenarios.
  • password: Also known as Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant. The application collects the user's username and password directly and exchanges them for an access token. This grant type should only be used when there is a high degree of trust between the user and the application, as it requires handling user credentials directly. Generally discouraged for security reasons unless legacy systems require it.
No client_credentials rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.client.id Client ID The client ID for OAuth 2.0 authentication. No - rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.client.secret Client Secret The client secret for OAuth 2.0 authentication. No - rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.username User Name Username required when using the password OAuth 2.0 grant type. No - rabbitmq.connection.oauth2.password Password Password required when using the password OAuth 2.0 grant type. No - Resilience rabbitmq.connection.idle.timeout Connection Idle Timeout Maximum period (in milliseconds) the connection can remain idle before being closed. No 60000 rabbitmq.connection.establish.retry.count Connection Establish Retry Count Number of times to retry establishing the connection. No 5 rabbitmq.connection.establish.retry.interval Connection Establish Retry Interval Interval (in milliseconds) between retries when establishing the connection. No 1000 rabbitmq.connection.recovery.policy.type Connection Recovery Policy Type Defines the strategy for automatic connection recovery after a disconnection. Options:
  • FIXED: Attempts to reconnect immediately after a connection failure with a fixed interval between retry attempts. This provides the fastest reconnection but may overwhelm the broker if it's experiencing issues or during network instability.
  • FIXED_WITH_INITIAL_DELAY: Waits for a specified initial delay before attempting the first reconnection, then continues with fixed intervals for subsequent retries. This gives the broker or network time to stabilize before reconnection attempts begin, reducing unnecessary load during transient failures.
  • FIXED_WITH_INITIAL_DELAY_AND_TIMEOUT: Combines an initial delay before the first retry attempt with a maximum timeout limit for the entire recovery process. If the connection cannot be re-established within the timeout period, recovery attempts cease. This prevents indefinite reconnection attempts and allows the application to fail gracefully or implement alternative handling. Recommended for production environments to balance resilience with resource management.
No FIXED_WITH_INITIAL_DELAY_AND_TIMEOUT rabbitmq.connection.recovery.initial.delay Connection Recovery Initial Delay Initial delay (in milliseconds) before the first recovery attempt starts. No 5000 rabbitmq.connection.recovery.retry.interval Connection Recovery Interval Fixed interval (in milliseconds) between connection recovery retries. No 10000 rabbitmq.connection.recovery.retry.timeout Connection Recovery Timeout Total time (in milliseconds) allowed for the connection recovery process before giving up. No 60000 Queue Properties rabbitmq.queue.arguments Arguments Additional arguments to customize queue behavior when declaring the queue. Specify as comma-separated key=value pairs (e.g., x-message-ttl=60000,x-max-length=1000). Common queue arguments:
  • x-message-ttl: Sets the time-to-live (TTL) for messages in milliseconds. Messages older than this value are automatically discarded or dead-lettered. Example: x-message-ttl=60000 (1 minute). Useful for time-sensitive data like session tokens or temporary notifications.
  • x-max-length: Limits the maximum number of messages the queue can hold. When exceeded, the overflow strategy (see queueOverflowStrategy) determines what happens. Example: x-max-length=10000. Prevents unbounded queue growth.
  • x-max-length-bytes: Limits the maximum total size of messages in bytes. Alternative to message count limit. Example: x-max-length-bytes=10485760 (10MB). Useful for controlling memory usage.
  • x-dead-letter-exchange: Specifies the exchange to route dead-lettered messages (expired, rejected, or exceeding delivery limits). Example: x-dead-letter-exchange=dlx. Essential for handling failed or problematic messages.
  • x-dead-letter-routing-key: Optional routing key for dead-lettered messages. If not set, the original routing key is used. Example: x-dead-letter-routing-key=failed.orders.
  • x-expires: Auto-deletes the queue after specified milliseconds of inactivity (no consumers, no messages published). Example: x-expires=1800000 (30 minutes). Useful for temporary or session-based queues.
  • x-single-active-consumer: When set to true, ensures only one consumer receives messages at a time (others are on standby). Example: x-single-active-consumer=true. Useful for ordered processing or leader election patterns.
Format: Use the syntax key1=value1,key2=value2 with no spaces. Numeric values should be in milliseconds for time-based arguments or plain integers/bytes for counts and sizes. Boolean values should be true or false. Note: Arguments specified here are applied during queue declaration. If the queue already exists with different arguments, the declaration will fail unless the arguments match exactly. Some arguments are queue-type specific (e.g., x-max-priority for CLASSIC queues only). Leave blank if no custom queue arguments are needed. No - rabbitmq.classic.version Queue Version For Classic Queues, select the queue implementation version. Options:
  • V1: The legacy classic queue implementation available in all RabbitMQ versions. Uses the original message storage and indexing mechanism. While mature and stable, it has known performance limitations with large queues, high message rates, and memory efficiency. Consider using V1 only for backward compatibility or if running RabbitMQ versions prior to 3.10.
  • V2: The modern classic queue implementation introduced in RabbitMQ 3.10, also known as CQv2 (Classic Queue version 2). Provides significantly improved performance, memory efficiency, and scalability through optimized message storage and reduced per-message overhead. Offers better handling of large queues (millions of messages) and higher throughput. Recommended for all new deployments and production workloads running RabbitMQ 3.10 or later. Note: Once a queue is created with a specific version, it cannot be changed without recreating the queue.
Important: This setting only applies to CLASSIC queue types and is ignored for QUORUM and STREAM queues. No - rabbitmq.classic.dead.letter.strategy Classic Queue Dead Letter Strategy For Classic Queues: defines the strategy for handling messages that fail processing and are negatively acknowledged or rejected. Options:
  • FIXED_DELAY_RETRYABLE_DISCARD: Implements an automatic retry mechanism with a fixed delay between retry attempts. When a message fails (discard), it is sent to a configured wait/delay queue where it waits for a specified period before being returned to the original queue for reprocessing. This retry cycle continues until either the message is successfully processed or the maximum dead-lettered count is reached, after which the message is routed to the final Dead Letter Queue for terminal handling. Required infrastructure:
    • A delay/wait queue with x-message-ttl argument for the retry delay period (e.g., 30000ms for 30-second delays)
    • Dead letter exchange routing configured on the delay queue to return messages to the original queue after TTL expiration
    • rabbitmq.max.dead.lettered.count to prevent infinite retry loops
    • Final DLQ infrastructure (rabbitmq.final.dead.letter.queue.name, rabbitmq.final.dead.letter.exchange.name) to capture poison messages
    Message flow:
    1. Message fails processing in original queue
    2. Dead-lettered to delay queue (with TTL)
    3. After TTL expires, message returns to original queue
    4. Retry processing attempt
    5. Repeat until success or max dead-lettered count reached
    6. If max count exceeded, route to final DLQ
    Use cases:
    • Transient failures: temporary network issues, rate limits, external service unavailability
    • Time-dependent processing: data not yet available but expected soon
    • Resource contention: database locks, API throttling that may clear with delay
    • Circuit breaker patterns: allowing time for downstream services to recover
    Provides automatic recovery without manual intervention but requires more complex infrastructure setup.
  • NON_RETRYABLE_DISCARD: No automatic retry mechanism. Messages that fail processing are immediately routed to the configured Dead Letter Exchange without any retry attempts. Failed messages move directly to the DLQ (via rabbitmq.dead.letter.exchange.name) or, if the max dead-lettered count is configured and exceeded, to the final DLQ. This is the simpler, more straightforward approach with minimal infrastructure requirements. Required infrastructure:
    • Dead Letter Exchange (rabbitmq.dead.letter.exchange.name)
    • Dead Letter Queue (rabbitmq.dead.letter.queue.name) bound to the DLX
    • Optional: Final DLQ infrastructure if using rabbitmq.max.dead.lettered.count
    Message flow:
    1. Message fails processing in original queue
    2. Immediately dead-lettered to DLX
    3. Routed to DLQ for manual review or alternative processing
    4. If max dead-lettered count configured and exceeded, routed to final DLQ instead
    Suitable for scenarios where:
    • Failures are permanent: invalid message format, schema violations, business rule violations that won't resolve with time
    • Retry logic is application-managed: consumer application implements its own retry strategy with more sophisticated logic
    • Manual intervention required: failed messages need human review, code fixes, or data corrections before reprocessing
    • Immediate failure notification needed: alerting and monitoring should trigger immediately without delay cycles
    • Simplicity preferred: avoiding the complexity of delay queue infrastructure
    This is the default and recommended option unless you specifically need automatic retry behavior with delays.
Strategy comparison: Aspect FIXED_DELAY_RETRYABLE_DISCARD NON_RETRYABLE_DISCARD Infrastructure complexity High (requires delay queues, additional DLX routing) Low (simple DLX → DLQ) Retry behavior Automatic with fixed delays None (immediate dead-lettering) Best for Transient failures, external service issues Permanent failures, application-managed retries Failure detection speed Delayed (after all retry attempts) Immediate Configuration requirements:
  • Both strategies work with the standard dead letter parameters: rabbitmq.dead.letter.exchange.name, rabbitmq.dead.letter.queue.name, etc.
  • FIXED_DELAY_RETRYABLE_DISCARD additionally requires manual setup of delay queues with TTL and proper DLX routing topology
  • Use rabbitmq.max.dead.lettered.count with both strategies to implement final DLQ routing and prevent infinite cycling
  • Configure retry delays via x-message-ttl on delay queues (not a connector parameter)
Important: This setting only applies to CLASSIC queue types and is ignored for QUORUM and STREAM queues. QUORUM queues use the rabbitmq.quorum.dead.letter.strategy parameter instead, which has different semantics (AT_MOST_ONCE vs AT_LEAST_ONCE delivery guarantees). No NON_RETRYABLE_DISCARD rabbitmq.classic.max.priority Max Priority For Classic Queues: defines the maximum priority level the queue should support (valid range: 0-255). When set, this parameter adds the x-max-priority argument to the queue declaration, enabling priority queue functionality. How it works: Messages published with a priority value (0 to the specified max) are delivered to consumers in priority order, with higher priority messages consumed first. Messages without an explicit priority are treated as priority 0 (lowest). Performance considerations: Priority queues have additional CPU and memory overhead compared to standard queues. Higher max priority values increase this overhead. For most use cases, a max priority of 10 or less is sufficient and recommended. Use cases: Suitable for scenarios requiring differentiated message handling, such as urgent alerts, high-priority transactions, or tiered job processing systems. Important: Priority queues are only supported by CLASSIC queues. This setting is ignored for QUORUM and STREAM queue types. Leave empty or set to 0 to disable priority functionality. No - rabbitmq.quorum.initial.member.count Initial Member Count Specifies the initial number of cluster nodes that will host replicas of the queue. This setting applies differently based on queue type: For Quorum Queues: Defines the initial replication factor (number of replica nodes) for the queue. The default is 3 replicas if not specified, which provides a good balance between availability and resource usage. Quorum queues require a majority (quorum) of replicas to be available for operation. For example, with 3 replicas, the queue tolerates 1 node failure; with 5 replicas, it tolerates 2 node failures. Higher replica counts improve fault tolerance but increase network overhead and resource consumption. For Stream Queues: Determines the initial number of stream replicas across cluster nodes. Similar to quorum queues, this affects data redundancy and availability. Streams use leader-based replication where one replica is the leader handling writes, while followers replicate data. Considerations:
  • The cluster must have at least as many nodes as the specified member count
  • Odd numbers (3, 5, 7) are recommended for quorum-based systems to avoid split-brain scenarios
  • Leave blank to use RabbitMQ's default behavior (typically 3 replicas)
Important: This setting only applies to QUORUM and STREAM queue types and is ignored for CLASSIC queues. No - rabbitmq.quorum.delivery.limit Delivery Limit For Quorum Queues: defines the maximum number of delivery attempts for a message before it is automatically dead-lettered or discarded. This setting adds the x-delivery-limit argument to the queue declaration. How it works: When a message is negatively acknowledged (discard) or requeued by a consumer, RabbitMQ increments its delivery counter. Once the delivery count reaches the specified limit, the message is either moved to a configured dead letter exchange (DLX) or dropped if no DLX is configured. Use cases: Prevents poison messages (messages that repeatedly fail processing) from blocking the queue indefinitely. Essential for building resilient systems where problematic messages can be isolated for manual inspection or alternative handling without affecting other messages. Best practices:
  • Always configure a dead letter exchange when using delivery limits to capture failed messages for analysis
  • Typical values range from 3-10 depending on your tolerance for retries
  • Consider implementing exponential backoff in consumers before relying solely on delivery limits
Important: This setting only applies to QUORUM queue types and is ignored for CLASSIC and STREAM queues. Leave blank to disable delivery limit enforcement (messages can be redelivered indefinitely). No - rabbitmq.quorum.dead.letter.strategy Quorum Queue Dead Letter Strategy For Quorum Queues: defines how messages are handled when being dead-lettered, controlling the delivery guarantee semantics. This setting adds the x-dead-letter-strategy argument to the queue declaration. Options:
  • AT_MOST_ONCE: The default and safer strategy. Messages are removed from the original queue before being published to the dead letter exchange (DLX). This guarantees that a message will not be duplicated if the dead-lettering process fails - it will either be in the original queue or successfully dead-lettered, but never in both. However, in case of broker failure during dead-lettering, the message may be lost. Recommended for most use cases where preventing duplicate processing is more critical than preventing message loss.
  • AT_LEAST_ONCE: Messages are published to the dead letter exchange first, then removed from the original queue only after successful publication. This ensures no message is lost during the dead-lettering process, but in case of failures, the same message might be dead-lettered multiple times, resulting in duplicates in the DLX. Use this when message loss is unacceptable and your downstream systems can handle duplicate messages (idempotent processing).
Trade-offs:
  • AT_MOST_ONCE: Prevents duplicates, risks message loss on failure
  • AT_LEAST_ONCE: Prevents message loss, risks duplicates on failure
Important: This setting only applies to QUORUM queue types and requires a dead letter exchange to be configured. It is ignored for CLASSIC and STREAM queues. No - rabbitmq.stream.initial.member.count Initial Member Count For STREAM queues: specifies the initial number of cluster nodes that will host replicas of the stream. This setting adds the x-initial-cluster-size argument to the stream queue declaration. How it works: Stream queues use leader-based replication where one replica serves as the leader handling all write operations, while follower replicas asynchronously replicate data for redundancy and availability. The initial member count determines how many replicas are created when the stream is first declared. Default behavior: If not specified, RabbitMQ uses a default value of 3 replicas, which provides a good balance between data safety and resource usage. With 3 replicas, the stream can tolerate the loss of up to 2 nodes while maintaining data availability (though writes require the leader to be available). Fault tolerance:
  • 1 replica: No redundancy - node failure results in data loss until recovery
  • 3 replicas: Tolerates 2 node failures for read operations; leader failure requires failover
  • 5 replicas: Higher redundancy but increased network and storage overhead
Considerations:
  • The cluster must have at least as many available nodes as the specified member count
  • Higher replica counts improve data durability but increase disk usage (each replica stores a complete copy) and network traffic (replication overhead)
  • Unlike quorum queues, streams don't require a quorum for operation - only the leader needs to be available for writes
  • Replicas can be added or removed after stream creation using RabbitMQ management commands
Important: This setting only applies to STREAM queue types and is ignored for CLASSIC and QUORUM queues. Leave blank to use the RabbitMQ default (3 replicas). No - rabbitmq.stream.max.age Max Age (Seconds) For STREAM queues: defines the maximum time-based retention period for messages in the stream. This setting adds the x-max-age argument to the queue declaration. How it works: Messages older than the specified age are automatically deleted from the stream to manage disk space. Age is calculated from the message timestamp. The retention policy is evaluated periodically, not in real-time, so messages may persist slightly beyond the specified age. Format: Specify the duration using time units:
  • Y - Years (e.g., 1Y)
  • M - Months (e.g., 3M)
  • D - Days (e.g., 7D)
  • h - Hours (e.g., 24h)
  • m - Minutes (e.g., 30m)
  • s - Seconds (e.g., 3600s)
Use cases: Essential for managing storage costs and compliance requirements in event streaming scenarios. For example, audit logs might retain data for 90 days, while real-time analytics streams might only need 24 hours. Considerations:
  • Can be combined with maxLengthBytes - whichever limit is reached first triggers deletion
  • Deleted messages cannot be recovered
  • Leave blank for unlimited retention (not recommended for production - may exhaust disk space)
Important: This setting only applies to STREAM queue types and is ignored for CLASSIC and QUORUM queues. No - rabbitmq.stream.max.segment.size Max Segment Size (Bytes) For STREAM queues: defines the maximum size in bytes for individual segment files in the stream's underlying storage. This setting adds the x-stream-max-segment-size-bytes argument to the queue declaration. How it works: RabbitMQ streams store messages in append-only segment files on disk. When a segment reaches the specified size, it is closed and a new segment is created. Smaller segments are rotated more frequently, while larger segments reduce the number of files but increase individual file sizes. Performance implications:
  • Smaller segments (e.g., 100MB-250MB): More frequent rotation, faster deletion of old data when retention policies apply, better for scenarios with frequent retention policy enforcement, but higher file system overhead
  • Larger segments (e.g., 500MB-1GB): Fewer files, reduced I/O overhead, better sequential write performance, but slower retention cleanup and potentially longer recovery times
Default behavior: If not specified, RabbitMQ uses a default value of 500MB (524,288,000 bytes), which balances performance and manageability for most workloads. Best practices:
  • Consider your retention period: shorter retention periods benefit from smaller segments for faster cleanup
  • Match to your message rate: high-throughput streams may benefit from larger segments
  • Ensure adequate disk I/O capacity for your chosen segment size
  • Typical range: 100MB to 1GB depending on workload characteristics
Important: This setting only applies to STREAM queue types and is ignored for CLASSIC and QUORUM queues. Leave blank to use the RabbitMQ default (500MB). No - rabbitmq.queue.exclusive Exclusive If enabled, the queue is deleted when the declaring connection closes. Only one consumer can use it. Purpose: Throttling prevents overwhelming downstream systems, controls resource consumption, enforces API rate limits, or ensures compliance with service-level agreements (SLAs) that specify maximum processing rates. Use cases:
  • External API rate limits: Processing messages that call third-party APIs with strict rate limits (e.g., 1000 calls/hour)
  • Database protection: Limiting write operations to prevent overloading databases during peak message volumes
  • Cost control: Capping processing rates to control consumption-based costs (API calls, cloud resources)
  • Quality of service: Ensuring fair resource allocation across multiple consumers or message types
  • Gradual rollout: Slowly ramping up processing during new feature deployments or system migrations
Behavior:
  • true: Message consumption is limited according to rabbitmq.throttle.mode, rabbitmq.throttle.timeUnit, and rabbitmq.throttle.count
  • false (default): No throttling applied - messages are consumed as fast as the consumer can process them
Important: Throttling affects consumer throughput and may cause queue backlog if message arrival rate exceeds the throttling limit. Monitor queue depth and adjust limits appropriately. No false rabbitmq.throttle.mode Throttling Mode Defines the strategy for applying rate limiting to message consumption. Options:
  • FIXED_INTERVAL: Enforces a fixed delay between consecutive message processing operations. The delay is calculated to achieve the target rate: delay = (timeUnit in ms) / count. For example, to process 60 messages/minute: delay = 60000ms / 60 = 1000ms between messages. Characteristics:
    • Smooth, evenly distributed message processing over time
    • Predictable, constant throughput rate
    • Each message incurs the calculated delay before the next message is fetched
    • More suitable for steady-state workloads with consistent message arrival rates
    Example: With 100 messages/minute setting:
    • Delay between messages: 600ms
    • Processing pattern: message → 600ms delay → message → 600ms delay → ...
    • Exactly 100 messages processed per minute, evenly spaced
    Best for: Scenarios requiring smooth, predictable load distribution; preventing burst traffic to downstream systems; strict timing requirements.
  • BATCH: Processes messages in bursts up to the specified count within each time window, then waits until the next time window begins. Messages are consumed rapidly until the batch limit is reached, followed by a pause until the time window resets. Characteristics:
    • Bursty processing pattern with idle periods
    • Processes messages as fast as possible until limit reached
    • After reaching count limit, waits for the time window to reset before processing more
    • More efficient for scenarios where downstream systems can handle bursts
    Example: With 100 messages/minute setting:
    • At minute start (0:00): rapidly process 100 messages (may take 5-10 seconds)
    • Remaining time (0:10 - 1:00): idle, waiting for next time window
    • At next minute (1:00): process next 100 messages
    Best for: Batch-oriented downstream systems; scenarios where burst processing is acceptable; maximizing throughput within rate limits while minimizing overall processing time. Default and recommended: BATCH mode is simpler and typically more efficient, as it minimizes the overhead of per-message delays while still respecting rate limits.
Mode comparison: Aspect FIXED_INTERVAL BATCH Processing pattern Evenly distributed over time Bursty with idle periods Downstream load Smooth, constant rate Burst at window start, then idle Latency More consistent per-message Variable (fast if within limit, delayed if limit reached) Efficiency Lower (constant delay overhead) Higher (processes at max speed within limits) Best for Steady load distribution, timing-sensitive operations Burst-tolerant systems, maximizing throughput Important: Only relevant when rabbitmq.throttle.enabled is true. The mode selection depends on downstream system characteristics and processing requirements. No BATCH rabbitmq.throttle.timeUnit Throttling Time Unit Defines the time window for applying the throttling rate limit. Combined with rabbitmq.throttle.count, this determines the maximum message processing rate. Options:
  • MINUTE: Rate limit is applied per 60-second window. The throttle count represents the maximum messages to process per minute. Use cases:
    • Short-term rate limits (typical for most API rate limits)
    • Fine-grained control over processing rates
    • Responsive throttling that adapts quickly to load changes
    Example: count=120, timeUnit=MINUTE → Maximum 120 messages per minute (2 messages/second average) FIXED_INTERVAL behavior: 60000ms / 120 = 500ms delay between messages BATCH behavior: Process up to 120 messages rapidly, then wait until next minute boundary
  • HOUR: Rate limit is applied per 60-minute window. The throttle count represents the maximum messages to process per hour. Use cases:
    • Hourly API quotas or service limits
    • Longer-term resource management
    • Systems with hourly billing or cost tracking
    Example: count=10000, timeUnit=HOUR → Maximum 10,000 messages per hour (≈167 messages/minute average) FIXED_INTERVAL behavior: 3600000ms / 10000 = 360ms delay between messages BATCH behavior: Process up to 10,000 messages rapidly at hour start, then wait until next hour
  • DAY: Rate limit is applied per 24-hour window. The throttle count represents the maximum messages to process per day. Use cases:
    • Daily quotas or processing limits
    • Long-term capacity planning and cost control
    • Systems with daily budget constraints
    • Compliance requirements with daily processing caps
    Example: count=100000, timeUnit=DAY → Maximum 100,000 messages per day (≈4167 messages/hour, ≈69 messages/minute average) FIXED_INTERVAL behavior: 86400000ms / 100000 = 864ms delay between messages BATCH behavior: Process up to 100,000 messages rapidly at day start, then wait until next day (midnight)
Choosing the right time unit:
  • Match downstream limits: If external API has 1000/hour limit, use HOUR with count=1000
  • Consider bursty behavior: Shorter time units (MINUTE) with BATCH mode create more frequent bursts; longer units (HOUR, DAY) create larger, less frequent bursts
  • Balance responsiveness: Shorter time units allow faster adaptation to changing conditions
  • Account for time zone resets: DAY-based throttling resets at midnight in the system timezone
Important: Only relevant when rabbitmq.throttle.enabled is true. The time unit should align with the rate limiting requirements of your downstream systems or organizational policies. No MINUTE rabbitmq.throttle.count Throttling Limit Specifies the maximum number of messages to process within the configured time unit. Combined with rabbitmq.throttle.timeUnit, this defines the target processing rate. How it works: The count determines either:
  • FIXED_INTERVAL mode: Used to calculate the delay between messages: delay = (timeUnit in milliseconds) / count
  • BATCH mode: The maximum number of messages to process before waiting for the next time window
Calculation examples:
  • count=60, timeUnit=MINUTE → 60 messages per minute = 1 message/second
    • FIXED_INTERVAL: 1000ms delay between messages
    • BATCH: Process 60 messages, wait until next minute
  • count=3600, timeUnit=HOUR → 3600 messages per hour = 1 message/second
    • FIXED_INTERVAL: 1000ms delay between messages
    • BATCH: Process 3600 messages, wait until next hour
  • count=10, timeUnit=MINUTE → 10 messages per minute = 1 message every 6 seconds
    • FIXED_INTERVAL: 6000ms delay between messages
    • BATCH: Process 10 messages rapidly, wait ~50+ seconds until next minute
Setting appropriate values:
  • Match external limits: If calling an API with 1000 requests/hour limit, set count to slightly below (e.g., 950) to provide safety margin
  • Consider processing time: Ensure the count allows enough time for actual message processing. For BATCH mode, count × avg_processing_time should be less than the time window
  • Account for multiple consumers: If multiple consumer instances are running, divide the total limit by the number of instances
  • Start conservative: Begin with lower counts and gradually increase based on monitoring and downstream system capacity
Impact on throughput:
  • Lower counts: More restrictive throttling, lower throughput, higher queue backlog risk, but better downstream protection
  • Higher counts: Less restrictive throttling, higher throughput, faster queue processing, but may stress downstream systems
Monitoring considerations:
  • Monitor queue depth to ensure throttling limits aren't causing excessive backlog
  • Track actual processing rates to verify throttling is working as expected
  • Alert on queue growth that exceeds normal thresholds
  • Adjust count dynamically based on downstream system health and capacity
Important: Required when rabbitmq.throttle.enabled is true. Must be a positive integer greater than 0. The effectiveness of throttling depends on proper alignment with downstream system capabilities and rate limits. No - Other rabbitmq.server.virtual.host Virtual Host The virtual host (vhost) to connect to. Leave blank for the default '/' vhost. No / rabbitmq.message.content.type Content-Type Specifies the default Content-Type header to apply to consumed messages when the content type cannot be determined from the message's properties. How it works: RabbitMQ messages can include a content_type property set by the publisher. If this property is missing or empty, the connector uses this default value to interpret and process the message body appropriately. Common values:
  • application/json: For JSON-formatted message bodies (most common for modern APIs and microservices)
  • application/xml: For XML-formatted message bodies
  • text/plain: For plain text messages
  • application/octet-stream: For binary data without specific format
  • application/x-www-form-urlencoded: For form-encoded data
Use cases:
  • Working with legacy systems that don't set content type properties
  • Enforcing a default format for all messages in a queue
  • Ensuring proper message deserialization when content type is ambiguous
Important: This value is only used as a fallback when the message doesn't have a content_type property. Messages with explicit content_type properties will use their own value. Leave blank if content type should always be determined from message properties (recommended when publishers consistently set this property). No - rabbitmq.message.content.encoding Content Encoding (Charset) Specifies the default character encoding/charset to use when decoding text-based message bodies if the encoding cannot be determined from the message's properties. How it works: RabbitMQ messages can include a content_encoding property set by the publisher indicating the character set (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1). If this property is missing, this default value is used to decode the message body bytes into text. Common values:
  • UTF-8: Universal character encoding supporting all languages (most common and recommended default)
  • ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1): Western European languages
  • US-ASCII: Basic ASCII characters only
  • UTF-16: Unicode encoding with 16-bit code units
Use cases:
  • Working with legacy publishers that don't set content encoding
  • Ensuring correct text decoding for international character sets
  • Preventing character corruption when processing multilingual messages
Considerations:
  • Incorrect encoding can cause character corruption, especially for non-ASCII characters (accents, emoji, non-Latin scripts)
  • UTF-8 is the safest default for modern applications as it supports all Unicode characters
  • This only affects text-based content types; binary data is not decoded
Important: This value is only used as a fallback when the message doesn't have a content_encoding property. Leave blank if encoding should always be determined from message properties (recommended when publishers consistently set this property). No - rabbitmq.queue.overflow.strategy Queue Overflow Strategy Defines the behavior when a queue reaches its maximum length limit (set via maxLength or maxLengthBytes). This setting adds the x-overflow argument to the queue declaration. Options:
  • DROP_HEAD: Automatically discards the oldest messages from the front of the queue to make room for new incoming messages. The queue maintains its maximum size by continuously dropping the oldest data. Publishers are not notified of the drops, and messages are silently discarded without any delivery guarantees. Best for scenarios where recent data is more valuable than old data, such as real-time metrics, live sensor readings, or recent activity feeds where historical data can be safely discarded.
  • REJECT_PUBLISH: Refuses to accept new messages when the queue is full. Publishers receive a negative acknowledgment (basic.return or exception depending on the client), allowing them to handle the rejection (retry, log error, route elsewhere). The queue preserves all existing messages without dropping any. Suitable for workloads where message loss is unacceptable and publishers can implement backpressure handling or alternative routing strategies.
  • REJECT_PUBLISH_DLX: Similar to REJECT_PUBLISH, but rejected messages are automatically routed to the configured Dead Letter Exchange (DLX) instead of being lost. This allows rejected messages to be captured, inspected, and potentially reprocessed later. Requires a DLX to be configured on the queue; otherwise, behaves like REJECT_PUBLISH. Ideal for critical workflows where overflow messages need preservation and manual review, or for implementing overflow queues as a secondary processing tier.
Use case guidance:
  • DROP_HEAD: Circular buffers, caching layers, monitoring dashboards, sliding time windows
  • REJECT_PUBLISH: Task queues with strict ordering, financial transactions, systems with explicit backpressure
  • REJECT_PUBLISH_DLX: Audit systems, compliance-sensitive workflows, overflow handling with recovery options
Important: This setting applies to CLASSIC and QUORUM queues when length limits are defined. STREAM queues handle overflow through their own retention mechanisms (maxAge, maxLengthBytes). This parameter is used when auto-declaring queues; for pre-existing queues, the overflow strategy must be set via queue arguments during queue creation. No DROP_HEAD rabbitmq.message.requeue.delay Requeue Delay Specifies the delay (in milliseconds) before a failed message is automatically requeued to the original queue for reprocessing. How it works: When a message processing fails and the consumer negatively acknowledges it (nack) with requeue=true, instead of immediately returning the message to the queue, the connector waits for this delay period before requeuing. This prevents rapid retry loops and gives time for transient issues to resolve. Use cases:
  • Transient failure handling: Temporary database connection issues, external service timeouts, rate limiting
  • Rate limiting: Preventing overwhelming of downstream services with rapid retries
  • Circuit breaker support: Allowing time for circuit breakers to reset or services to recover
  • Resource contention: Giving time for locks to release or resources to become available
Typical values:
  • 0-1000ms (0-1 second): Quick retry for very transient failures
  • 5000-10000ms (5-10 seconds): Moderate delay for service recovery
  • 30000-60000ms (30-60 seconds): Longer delay for persistent transient issues
Considerations:
  • During the delay, the message is held by the consumer and counts against the prefetch limit
  • Longer delays reduce retry storms but increase message processing latency
  • This is a simple fixed delay; for exponential backoff, consider using the FIXED_DELAY_RETRYABLE_DISCARD strategy with delay queues
  • If rabbitmq.auto.ack.enabled is true, this setting has no effect as messages are auto-acknowledged
Important: Leave blank or set to 0 for immediate requeue (no delay). This setting only applies when messages are nacked with requeue=true. For more sophisticated retry patterns with exponential backoff, use dead letter exchanges with TTL-based delay queues. No - rabbitmq.auto.ack.enabled Auto Acknowledge Enabled Controls whether messages are automatically acknowledged immediately upon delivery to the consumer, before processing begins. Behavior:
  • false (default, recommended): Manual acknowledgment mode. Messages are acknowledged only after successful processing by the application. If processing fails or the consumer crashes, unacknowledged messages are automatically requeued by RabbitMQ, ensuring at-least-once delivery. Provides reliability and message safety at the cost of requiring explicit acknowledgment handling.
  • true: Automatic acknowledgment mode. RabbitMQ considers messages acknowledged as soon as they're delivered to the consumer, regardless of processing outcome. If the consumer crashes or processing fails after delivery, the message is lost permanently. Provides higher throughput and simpler code but risks message loss. Only use when message loss is acceptable.
Trade-offs: Aspect Auto ACK (true) Manual ACK (false) Reliability Low - message loss on failures High - at-least-once delivery Performance Higher throughput Slightly lower (ACK overhead) Code complexity Simpler (no ACK handling) More complex (explicit ACK/NACK) Message reprocessing Not possible Automatic on failure When to use auto ACK (true):
  • Logs, metrics, or monitoring data where loss is acceptable
  • Duplicate-sensitive workflows where at-most-once delivery is required
  • High-throughput scenarios where performance outweighs reliability
  • Development/testing environments
When to use manual ACK (false, recommended):
  • Financial transactions, orders, payments, or any critical business data
  • State changes that must not be lost
  • Production systems where message reliability is important
  • Scenarios requiring retry on failure
Important: When auto ACK is enabled, settings like rabbitmq.message.requeue.delay, rabbitmq.ack.wait.time, and dead letter strategies have reduced or no effect since messages are acknowledged before processing. No false rabbitmq.ack.wait.time ACKNOWLEDGE Wait Time (ms) Defines the maximum time (in milliseconds) to wait for message processing to complete before timing out the acknowledgment operation. How it works: In manual acknowledgment mode (rabbitmq.auto.ack.enabled=false), after delivering a message to the consumer application, the connector waits up to this duration for the application to process the message and send an acknowledgment (ACK or NACK). If processing exceeds this timeout, the connector may take timeout action depending on implementation (typically logging an error and potentially nacking the message). Purpose:
  • Prevents indefinite blocking when message processing hangs or takes unexpectedly long
  • Allows detection of slow or stuck message processing
  • Ensures system responsiveness and resource cleanup
  • Helps identify performance bottlenecks or processing issues
Typical values:
  • 30000-60000ms (30-60 seconds): For quick processing tasks (API calls, simple transformations)
  • 180000ms (3 minutes): Default - suitable for moderate processing complexity
  • 300000-600000ms (5-10 minutes): For complex processing, external service calls, or batch operations
  • 900000ms+ (15+ minutes): For very long-running tasks, though these may be better handled asynchronously
Considerations:
  • Should be longer than your worst-case expected processing time plus buffer
  • Too short: legitimate long-running tasks may timeout and be requeued unnecessarily
  • Too long: hung processes won't be detected promptly, tying up resources
  • Monitor actual processing times to tune appropriately
  • Consider breaking very long tasks into smaller chunks or using async patterns
Important: This setting only applies when rabbitmq.auto.ack.enabled=false (manual acknowledgment mode). In auto ACK mode, messages are acknowledged immediately upon receipt, so this timeout is not relevant. Timeout behavior may vary by connector implementation - consult specific connector documentation. No 180000 rabbitmq.concurrent.consumers.count Concurrent Consumers Specifies the number of concurrent consumer instances to create for processing messages from the queue in parallel. How it works: Each consumer runs independently and can process messages simultaneously. RabbitMQ distributes messages across all active consumers using round-robin (by default) or other distribution strategies. Multiple consumers enable parallel processing and higher throughput. Benefits of multiple consumers:
  • Increased throughput: Process more messages per second by parallelizing work
  • Better resource utilization: Keep CPUs busy while waiting on I/O operations
  • Fault tolerance: If one consumer fails, others continue processing
  • Reduced latency: Messages don't wait in queue as long when more consumers are available
Typical values:
  • 1: Single consumer - simplest configuration, ordered processing, lower throughput
  • 2-10: Moderate parallelism - good balance for most workloads
  • 10-50+: High parallelism - for high-volume queues or I/O-bound processing
Considerations:
  • Message ordering: Multiple consumers break message ordering within the queue. If strict ordering is required, use 1 consumer or implement application-level ordering
  • Resource consumption: Each consumer uses memory, threads, and connections. Scale based on available resources
  • Prefetch interaction: Works with rabbitmq.consumer.initial.credit (prefetch). Total in-flight messages = consumers × prefetch
  • Thread pool sizing: Should coordinate with rabbitmq.message.receiver.thread.pool.size - thread pool should be ≥ concurrent consumers
  • Bottleneck identification: If processing is CPU-bound, more consumers help. If I/O-bound (databases, APIs), many consumers increase parallelism
Scaling guidance:
  • Start with 2-4 consumers and monitor queue depth and processing latency
  • Increase if queue depth grows despite available CPU/memory
  • Decrease if consumers are often idle or resource usage is excessive
  • For I/O-bound tasks, can use more consumers than CPU cores
  • For CPU-bound tasks, match consumer count to available cores
Important: Changes require application restart to take effect. For dynamic scaling based on queue depth, consider using RabbitMQ autoscaling features or container orchestration (Kubernetes HPA). No 1 rabbitmq.message.receiver.thread.pool.size Message Receiver Thread Pool Size Defines the size of the thread pool dedicated to receiving and initially processing messages from RabbitMQ. This thread pool handles message delivery from the broker to the consumer application. How it works: RabbitMQ client libraries use threads to handle network I/O and message delivery. This parameter controls how many threads are available for these operations, enabling concurrent message receipt and processing. Relationship with concurrent consumers:
  • Thread pool size should generally be greater than or equal to concurrent consumer count
  • Each consumer may use one or more threads from this pool
  • Insufficient threads can bottleneck message delivery even if consumers are idle
  • Recommended: thread pool size ≥ concurrent consumers (often 1.5-2× concurrent consumers)
Typical configurations: Concurrent Consumers Recommended Thread Pool Size Rationale 1 1-2 Minimal overhead 5 5-10 1-2 threads per consumer 10 15-20 Buffer for peak loads 20+ 30-50+ High concurrency workloads Considerations:
  • Too small: Message delivery bottleneck, consumers starved of messages, reduced throughput
  • Too large: Excessive memory usage (each thread consumes stack memory), potential thread contention
  • I/O-bound vs CPU-bound: I/O-bound processing benefits from larger thread pools; CPU-bound may not
  • Memory impact: Each thread typically uses 1MB+ of stack space (platform-dependent)
Tuning guidance:
  • Start with thread pool = 2 × concurrent consumers
  • Monitor thread utilization and message delivery latency
  • Increase if thread pool exhaustion is observed (blocked message delivery)
  • Decrease if excessive idle threads or memory pressure occurs
Important: This controls the connector's internal threading, not the application's business logic thread pool. Business logic may run on separate threads or executors depending on the connector implementation. No 1 rabbitmq.consumer.initial.credit Consumer Initial Credit Defines the prefetch count (QoS - Quality of Service) limit, controlling the maximum number of unacknowledged messages that can be delivered to a single consumer at once. How it works: RabbitMQ uses a credit-based flow control mechanism. Each consumer is allocated an initial credit (prefetch count). The broker delivers messages up to this limit before pausing delivery. As the consumer acknowledges messages, credit is replenished and more messages are delivered. This prevents consumers from being overwhelmed with messages. Impact on system behavior:
  • Load balancing: With multiple consumers, lower prefetch ensures more even distribution (each consumer gets fewer messages at once). Higher prefetch may cause uneven load (fast consumers get many messages, slow ones get few)
  • Throughput: Higher prefetch increases throughput by reducing round-trips to the broker and keeping consumers continuously busy
  • Latency: Lower prefetch reduces message latency (messages don't wait in consumer buffers as long)
  • Memory usage: Higher prefetch increases consumer memory usage (more messages buffered in-flight)
  • Failure impact: Higher prefetch means more messages are redelivered if consumer crashes (all unacknowledged messages)
Typical values:
  • 1: Strict round-robin distribution, minimal memory, highest latency, lowest throughput. Best for ensuring fair load distribution or when message processing is very slow and inconsistent
  • 10-50: Balanced approach - good throughput with reasonable memory usage and load distribution. Suitable for most workloads
  • 100-1000: High throughput scenarios where consumers can handle large batches efficiently. Best when processing time is consistent and fast
  • 0 (unlimited): No limit - broker sends all available messages. Risky - can cause out-of-memory errors. Only for specific scenarios with known bounded queue sizes
Calculation with multiple consumers:
  • Total in-flight messages = concurrent consumers × prefetch count
  • Example: 5 consumers × 20 prefetch = 100 messages in-flight maximum
  • Ensure total doesn't exceed available memory and processing capacity
Tuning guidance: Scenario Recommended Prefetch Variable processing time (some messages slow, some fast) 1-10 (ensures fair distribution) Consistent fast processing (< 100ms per message) 50-100 (maximize throughput) I/O-bound processing (API calls, database queries) 20-50 (balance parallelism and memory) Large messages (MB+ size) 1-5 (limit memory consumption) Critical ordering requirements 1 (with 1 consumer) Important: This is a per-consumer setting. Each consumer gets this prefetch limit independently. For auto-ack mode (rabbitmq.auto.ack.enabled=true), prefetch still applies but has less impact since messages are immediately acknowledged upon delivery. No 1 rabbitmq.classic.override.requeue.with.discard Override Requeue Decision With Discard For Classic Queues: controls whether requeue attempts for failed messages are overridden and converted to discard/dead-letter operations instead. Behavior:
  • false (default): Normal requeue behavior - when a message is negatively acknowledged (nack) with requeue=true, it is returned to the queue for redelivery. The message can be reprocessed by the same or different consumer.
  • true: Override mode - any requeue attempt (nack with requeue=true) is converted to a discard operation. Instead of returning to the queue, the message is:
    • Routed to the configured Dead Letter Exchange (if rabbitmq.dead.letter.exchange.name is set)
    • Discarded entirely if no DLX is configured
    This effectively disables requeuing for the queue, forcing all failed messages to follow the dead letter path.
Use cases for enabling (true):
  • Prevent infinite loops: When messages consistently fail and requeuing causes endless retry cycles
  • Poison message protection: Immediately route problematic messages to DLQ for inspection rather than reprocessing
  • Enforce dead letter workflow: Ensure all failures go through the dead letter mechanism for consistent handling
  • Debugging and monitoring: Capture all failed messages in DLQ for analysis without reprocessing noise
  • Complement to delivery limits: Work with delivery limit settings to ensure messages don't cycle indefinitely
Relationship with other settings:
  • Works in conjunction with rabbitmq.classic.dead.letter.strategy
  • Requires rabbitmq.dead.letter.exchange.name to be configured for failed messages to be captured (otherwise they're lost)
  • Interacts with rabbitmq.message.requeue.delay - when override is enabled, the delay is bypassed as messages aren't requeued
  • Most useful with NON_RETRYABLE_DISCARD strategy for immediate failure handling
Considerations:
  • Message loss risk: If DLX is not configured and this is true, all requeue attempts result in permanent message loss
  • No retry opportunity: Transient failures that might succeed on retry will instead be dead-lettered immediately
  • Monitoring importance: Essential to monitor DLQ when this is enabled, as all failures accumulate there
Example scenarios: Setting Message Processing Fails Consumer Action Result false (default) Consumer nacks with requeue=true Request requeue Message requeued for retry true Consumer nacks with requeue=true Request requeue Message discarded/dead-lettered (requeue overridden) true or false Consumer nacks with requeue=false Request discard Message discarded/dead-lettered (same behavior) Important: This setting only applies to CLASSIC queue types and is ignored for QUORUM and STREAM queues. Always configure a Dead Letter Exchange when enabling this to prevent message loss. This is a safety mechanism - use with caution and ensure DLQ monitoring is in place. No false

docs.title: Setting up the Redis Environment
docs.text: The Redis connector allows you to access the Redis commands from an integration sequence. Redis stands for remote dictionary server. Redis store/server that stores data as key-value pairs and this key-value store can be used as a database.

docs.title: Setting up the environment
docs.text:
Before you start configuring the Redis connector, you need the WSO2 integration runtime. Download the integration runtime and extract the ZIP file to a known location. In this setup guide we refer to that location as <PRODUCT_HOME>.

To configure the Redis connector, download the following client libraries from the given locations and copy to the <PRODUCT_HOME>/lib directory.

  • For Redis connector v1.0.1 - jedis-2.1.0.jar
  • For Redis connector v2.1.x and above - jedis-3.6.0.jar

docs.title: Setting up the Redis server
docs.text:
1. Download the Redis server and follow the steps given in this page to install this in your local machine.
  2. After setting up the Redis Server, navigate to the location you installed Redis and execute the sudo make install command.
  3. Enter redis-server command to start the Redis server.

  4. In the command line, you can see the Redis port and PID as shown below.

  5. You can interact with Redis using the built-in client. In the command line, navigate to the location you installed Redis. Enter redis-cli.

docs.title: Redis Connector Example
docs.text: The Redis connector allows you to access the Redis commands from an integration sequence.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
Given below is a sample scenario that demonstrates how to work with the WSO2 Redis Connector and access the Redis server, using Redis commands.

The user sends the request to invoke an API to get stock details. This REST call will get converted into a SOAP message and is sent to the back-end service. While the response from the backend service is converted back to JSON and sent back to the API caller, the integration runtime will extract stock volume details from the response and store it into a configured Redis server. When users need to retrieve stock volumes collected, they can invoke the getstockvolumedetails resource. This example also demonstrates how users can manipulate stock volume details by removing unwanted items from the Redis server.

Note: In this scenario you need to set up the Redis Server in your local machine. Please refer to the Setting up the Redis Connector documentation. Follow the steps listed under Setting up the Redis server section to setup the Redis server and Set up the back-end service section to setup the Stockquote service. This example demonstrates how to use Redis connector to:

  1. Retrieve stock volume details from the Stockquote back-end service. This is done while extracting the stock volume, creating a Redis hash map, and adding stock volume details to the Redis server. (In this example, Redis hashes are used to store different companies' stock volume details. Since the “symbol” that is sent in the request is “WSO2”, the request is routed to the WSO2 endpoint. Once the response from the WSO2 endpoint is received, it is transformed according to the specified template and sent to the client. Then create a hash map and insert extracted details into the Redis hashmap).
  2. Retrieve all stock volume details from the Redis server.
  3. Remove stock volume details from the Redis server.

All three operations are exposed via a StockQuoteAPI API. The API with the context /stockquote has three resources:

  • /getstockquote/{symbol}: This is used to get stock volume details while extracting and sending details to the Redis hash map.
  • /getstockvolumedetails : Retrieve information about the inserted stock volume details.
  • /deletestockvolumedetails : Remove unwanted stock volume details.

The following diagram shows the overall solution. The user creates a hash map, stores WSO2 stock volume details into the list, and then receives it back and removes unwanted hash map items. To invoke each operation, the user uses the same API.

If you do not want to configure this yourself, you can simply get the project and run it.

docs.title: Setup the Integration Project
docs.text:
1. Launch Visual Studio Code with the WSO2 Integrator: MI for VS Code extension (MI for VS Code) installed.

    Info

    Follow the Install WSO2 Integrator: MI for VS Code documentation for a complete installation guide.

  2. Create an integration project.

docs.title: Create the Endpoint
docs.text:
1. Navigate to MI Project Explorer > Endpoints and click on the + icon next to Endpoints.

  2. Select Address Endpoint.

  3. In Endpoint Artifact interface that appears, specify the following values and click Create.

    Parameter Value Endpoint Name StockQuoteEP URI Template http://localhost:9000/services/SimpleStockQuoteService Format SOAP 1.1

docs.title: Create the REST API
docs.text:
1. Navigate to MI Project Explorer > APIs and click on the + sign next to APIs to open the Synapse API Artifact creation form.

  2. Specify the API name as SampleRedisAPI and the API context as /stockquote and click Create.

    After creating the API artifact, the Service Designer pane will be displayed with the default API resource.

docs.title: Configure a resource for the getstockquote operation
docs.text:
Configure a resource that sets up a Redis hash map and sets a specific field in a hash to a specified value. In this sample, the user sends the request to invoke the created API to get WSO2 stock volume details. To achieve this, follow the steps below.

  1. Click on the GET getstockquote API resource under available resources on the Service Designer.

    You will now see the graphical view of the SampleRedisAPI.

  2. Click on the + icon under start to add a mediator.

  3. Add a Payload mediator from the mediator palette to extract the selected stock details. In this sample, we attempt to get WSO2 stock details from the SimpleStockQuoteService. Parameter Value Payload Format Inline Media Type xml Template Type default Payload 

    <m0:getQuote xmlns:m0="http://services.samples">
<m0:request>
<m0:symbol>$1</m0:symbol>
</m0:request>
</m0:getQuote>

    Add parameter: Argument value (Expression) get-property('uri.var.symbol') Evaluator xml

  4. Add a header to get a quote from the SimpleStockQuoteService.

    Parameter Value Header Name Action Header Action set Scope default Header Value Type LITERAL Header Value Literal urn:getQuote

  5. Add an address endpoint using the call mediator to access SimpleStockQuoteService. Select the previously created StockQuoteEP from the dropdown.

  6. In this example, we copy the original payload to a property using the Enrich mediator.

  7. To get the input values into the hSet, we can use the property mediator. Navigate into the Mediator Palette and select the Property mediators.

  8. Add the property mediator to capture the symbol value from the response of SimpleStockQuoteService. The 'symbol' contains the company name of the stock quote.

    Property Name symbol Property Value (Expression) $body/soapenv:Envelope/soapenv:Body/ns:getQuoteResponse/ax21:symbol

  9. Add the property mediator to capture the volume values. The 'volume' contains the stock quote volume of the selected company.

    Property Name volume Property Value (Expression) $body/soapenv:Envelope/soapenv:Body/ns:getQuoteResponse/ax21:volume

  10. Add Redis connector operation.

    1. Click + icon under the property mediator.

    2. Select the Redis connector from the Connectors section.

    3. Select hSet from the connector operations.

    4. Next, you have to create a Redis connection. Click the Add new connection.

    5. Configure the values as shown below and click Add.

      redisHost The Redis hostname (default: localhost) redisPort The port on which the Redis server is running (default: 6379)

    6. Navigate to the Add hSet form and select the created redis connection from the Connection Type dropdown.

    7. In this operation we are going to set a hash map to the Redis server. The hSet operation sets a specific field in a hash to a specified value.

      • redisKey : The name of the key where the hash is stored.
      • redisField : The field for which you want to set a value.
      • redisValue : The value that you want to set for the field.

      Configure the following values and click submit redisKey StockVolume redisField ctx:symbol</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td>redisValue</td> <td><code>ctx:volume

      In this example, the redisKey value is configured as StockVolume. While invoking the API, the above redisField, redisValue parameter values are extracted from the response of the SimpleStockQuoteService. Then they are populated as an input value for the Redis hSet operation.

  11. Then, to get the original payload, we replace the message body with the property value using the Enrich mediator as follows.

  12. Forward the backend response to the API caller.

    When you are invoking the created resource, the request of the message is going through the /getstockquote resource. Finally, it is passed to the Respond mediator. The Respond Mediator stops the processing of the current message and sends the message back to the client as a response.

    1. Add the respond mediator to the Resource view.

    2. Once you have setup the resource, you can see the getstockquote resource as shown below.

docs.title: Configure a resource for the getstockvolumedetails operation
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Service Designer view of the API and select the getstockvolumedetails resource.

  2. Click + under start and select the Redis connector from the Connectors section.

  3. Select hGetAll from the connector operations.

  4. Select REDIS_CONNECTION_1 from the connection dropdown.

docs.title: Configure a resource for the deletestockvolumedetails operation
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Service Designer view of the API and select the deletestockvolumedetails resource.

  2. Click the + under the start and select the Redis connector from the Connectors section.

  3. Select hDel from the connector operations. This operation deletes one or more hash fields

  4. Select REDIS_CONNECTION_1 from the connection dropdown.

  5. Configure the values.

    redisKey StockVolume redisFields $ctx:redisFields

  6. To forward the backend response to the API caller add the Respond Mediator.

Now you can switch to the Source view and check the XML configuration files of the created API and endpoint.

StockQuoteAPI.xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
    <api context="/stockquote" name="StockQuoteAPI" xmlns="http://ws.apache.org/ns/synapse">
        <resource methods="GET" uri-template="/getstockquote/{symbol}">
            <inSequence>
            <payloadFactory media-type="xml" template-type="default">
                <format>
                    <m0:getQuote xmlns:m0="http://services.samples">
                        <m0:request>
                            <m0:symbol>$1</m0:symbol>
                        </m0:request>
                    </m0:getQuote>
                </format>
                <args>
                    <arg evaluator="xml" expression="get-property('uri.var.symbol')"/>
                </args>
            </payloadFactory>
            <header name="Action" action="set" scope="default" value="urn:getQuote"/>
            <call>
                <endpoint key="StockQuoteEP"/>
            </call>
            <enrich description="">
                <source clone="true" type="body"/>
                <target action="replace" type="property" property="ORIGINAL_PAYLOAD"/>
            </enrich>
            <property name="symbol" scope="default" type="STRING" expression="$body/soapenv:Envelope/soapenv:Body/ns:getQuoteResponse/ax21:symbol" xmlns:ax21="http://services.samples/xsd" xmlns:ns="http://services.samples" xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"/>
            <property name="volume" scope="default" type="STRING" expression="$body/soapenv:Envelope/soapenv:Body/ns:getQuoteResponse/ax21:volume" xmlns:ax21="http://services.samples/xsd" xmlns:ns="http://services.samples" xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"/>
            <redis.hSet configKey="REDIS_CONNECTION_1">
                <redisKey>StockVolume</redisKey>
                <redisField>{$ctx:symbol}</redisField>
                <redisValue>{$ctx:volume}</redisValue>
            </redis.hSet>
            <enrich description="">
                <source clone="true" property="ORIGINAL_PAYLOAD" type="property"/>
                <target action="replace" type="body"/>
            </enrich>
            <log category="INFO" level="simple"/>
            <respond/>
        </inSequence>
            <faultSequence>
        </faultSequence>
        </resource>
        <resource methods="GET" uri-template="/getstockvolumedetails">
            <inSequence>
                <redis.hGetAll configKey="REDIS_CONNECTION_1">
                    <redisKey>StockVolume</redisKey>
                </redis.hGetAll>
                <respond/>
            </inSequence>
            <faultSequence/>
        </resource>
        <resource methods="POST" uri-template="/deletestockvolumedetails">
            <inSequence>
                <property expression="json-eval($.redisFields)" name="redisFields" scope="default" type="STRING"/>
            <redis.hDel configKey="REDIS_CONNECTION_1">
                <redisKey>StockVolume</redisKey>
                <redisFields>{$ctx:redisFields}</redisFields>
            </redis.hDel>
                <respond/>
            </inSequence>
            <faultSequence/>
        </resource>
    </api>

StockQuoteEP Endpoint 

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<endpoint name="StockQuoteEP" xmlns="http://ws.apache.org/ns/synapse">
<address format="soap11"    uri="http://localhost:9000/services/SimpleStockQuoteService">
<suspendOnFailure>
<initialDuration>-1</initialDuration>
<progressionFactor>1</progressionFactor>
</suspendOnFailure>
<markForSuspension>
<retriesBeforeSuspension>0</retriesBeforeSuspension>
</markForSuspension>
</address>
</endpoint>

REDIS_CONNECTION_1

The created Redis connection will be saved as a local entry.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<localEntry key="REDIS_CONNECTION_1" xmlns="http://ws.apache.org/ns/synapse">
<redis.init>
<connectionType>REDIS</connectionType>
<name>REDIS_CONNECTION_1</name>
<redisHost>127.0.0.1</redisHost>
<redisPort>6379</redisPort>
</redis.init>
</localEntry>

docs.title: Redis Connector Overview
docs.text:
Redis is an open source (BSD licensed), in-memory data structure store, used as a cache or a database, cache and message broker. It supports data structures such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets with range queries, bitmaps, hyperlogs and geospatial indexes with radius queries.

This connector enables developers to use an external Redis server as a cache or a database in the mediation logic.

Go to the WSO2 Connector Store to download the Redis connector.
